title: Kinetic Fluctuation-Dissipation Relation in collisionless plasmas: a correlated noise source
summary: We here focus on small-scale dynamics of collisionless plasmas by employing a generalized kinetic Langevin framework driven by a stochastic time-correlated forcing. Our investigation captures the steady-state Fluctuation-Dissipation Relation (FDR) where the energy injection at low frequencies is due to the time-correlated forcing and the small-scale energy conversion occurs via Landau damping, the latter --though formally reversible-- acting as an effective dissipation mechanism. We analytically extract the resulting asymptotic spectral scalings across multiple physical regimes and characterize the velocity-space cascade by decomposing the plasma distribution function with Hermite polynomials. The framework is then generalized to a multi-scale forcing scenario in which correlation rates are distributed according to a power-law distribution. This extension provides closed-form analytical expressions that may serve to interpret spacecraft in-situ observations. All analytical predictions are successfully validated through direct numerical integrations of the underlying kinetic equations.

AI.motivation: The study is motivated by the need to understand small-scale dynamics of collisionless plasmas, including energy injection, energy conversion, spectral behavior, and velocity-space cascades, and to provide closed-form expressions that may help interpret spacecraft in-situ observations.
AI.method: The authors employ a generalized kinetic Langevin framework driven by stochastic time-correlated forcing. title: Evaluation of Transverse Incoherent Tune Shifts in the Electron-Ion Collider
summary:
Achieving the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) peak luminosity goal of 10 to the power of 34 per square centimeter per second requires high average currents, flat beams, non-circular vacuum chambers, and large transverse orbit offsets in the Hadron Storage Ring (HSR) and Electron Storage Ring (ESR). These conditions can generate collective effects and incoherent tune spreads that drive particles across low-order betatron resonances, causing emittance growth, halo formation, and reduced beam lifetime.
  We quantitatively evaluate incoherent transverse betatron tune shifts from beam-beam interactions, direct space charge, and beam-environment interactions associated with image forces and vacuum chamber geometry. Xsuite and PyHEADTAIL simulations validate the analytical calculations for beam-beam and direct space-charge effects, respectively. For indirect space-charge effects, we review and compare several analytical formalisms and apply the Laslett image-charge formulation to rectangular vacuum chambers with off-axis beams. The analysis accounts for transverse orbit offsets of up to 20 mm in the HSR and 10 mm in the ESR.
  The results establish baseline parameters and provide quantitative guidance for EIC design, optimization, and operation. The comparison of indirect space-charge formalisms also offers an accessible reference and methodology for studies of high-intensity beam dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper quantifies incoherent transverse betatron tune shifts for the EIC Hadron and Electron Storage Rings arising from beam-beam interactions, direct space charge, and indirect space-charge/image effects in non-circular chambers with off-axis beams, using analytical calculations validated by Xsuite and PyHEADTAIL simulations where applicable.
AI.motivation: The EIC peak luminosity goal of 10^34 cm^-2 s^-1 requires high average currents, flat beams, non-circular vacuum chambers, and large transverse orbit offsets, which can produce collective effects and incoherent tune spreads that drive particles across low-order betatron resonances, leading to emittance growth, halo formation, and reduced beam lifetime.
AI.method: The authors quantitatively evaluate incoherent transverse betatron tune shifts from beam-beam interactions, direct space charge, and beam-environment interactions related to image forces and vacuum-chamber geometry. Xsuite and PyHEADTAIL simulations are used to validate analytical calculations for beam-beam and direct space-charge effects, respectively. For indirect space-charge effects, several analytical formalisms are reviewed and compared, and the Laslett image-charge formulation is applied to rectangular vacuum chambers with off-axis beams, accounting for transverse orbit offsets of up to 20 mm in the HSR and 10 mm in the ESR.

The comparison of indirect space-charge formalisms provides an accessible reference and methodology for high-intensity beam-dynamics studies. Specific numerical tune-shift values are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Incoherent transverse betatron tune shifts from beam-beam, direct space-charge, and indirect space-charge/image effects are relevant to EIC performance under its required high-current, flat-beam, non-circular-chamber, and large-offset conditions; the presented analytical and simulation framework supports EIC design and operation and offers a comparative methodology for indirect space-charge studies.

title: Oscillation modes, Decoherence, Beam Transfer Functions, and Instabilities for a Beam Subjected to Space-Charge Forces
summary: Based on the oscillation modes of a bunch subject to the space-charge force, we discuss the decoherence of the dipole oscillation, the beam transfer function, and the beam instability. The longitudinal phase space is discretized into \(n_l\times n_J\) grids in the azimuthal and radial directions, respectively. The transverse dipole moment in the longitudinal phase space is represented by a vector of length \(n_l n_J\), and the transformation given by the Vlasov equation is represented by a matrix transformation of size \(n_l n_J\times n_l n_J\). Solving the eigenvalue problem of this matrix gives the \(n_l n_J\) eigen-oscillation modes of the bunch. Using the resulting eigenvectors within a standard linear-algebraic treatment, we analyze these three phenomena. The analysis was performed for the Rapid Cycling Synchrotron (RCS) of the China Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS) using \(n_l=41\) and \(n_J=40\), and it visualizes the features related to the continuous distribution of the tune, Landau damping, and isolated modes separated from the continuous tune region.

AI.tldr: A discretized Vlasov eigenmode matrix method is used to analyze dipole decoherence, the beam transfer function, and beam instability for a space-charge-affected bunch, with application to the CSNS RCS using a 41×40 longitudinal phase-space grid.
AI.motivation: To discuss the decoherence of dipole oscillation, the beam transfer function, and beam instability based on the oscillation modes of a bunch subject to the space-charge force.
AI.method: The longitudinal phase space is discretized into n_l×n_J grids in azimuthal and radial directions; the transverse dipole moment is represented as a vector of length n_l n_J; the Vlasov-equation transformation is represented by an n_l n_J×n_l n_J matrix; solving its eigenvalue problem gives n_l n_J eigen-oscillation modes; the eigenvectors are used in a standard linear-algebraic treatment to analyze the three phenomena. The analysis is applied to the Rapid Cycling Synchrotron of the China Spallation Neutron Source with n_l=41 and n_J=40.

AI.conclusion: The matrix eigenmode approach provides a linear-algebraic framework for analyzing dipole decoherence, the beam transfer function, and beam instability; its application to the CSNS RCS visualizes tune-distribution, Landau-damping, and isolated-mode features, with no further quantitative conclusions provided in the abstract.

title: Development of a Prototype Superconducting Radio-Frequency Multicell Cavity for Compact, Conduction-Cooled Accelerators
summary: Jefferson Lab and General Atomics are jointly advancing compact, high-power irradiation systems capable of delivering electron-beam powers in the hundreds of kilowatts based on superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) technology. A critical step toward deploying SRF accelerators in industrial environments is replacing traditional liquid-helium cryogenic systems with conduction-cooled cryomodules powered by commercial cryocoolers. This paper reports recent progress in the design, fabrication, and testing of a prototype three-cell SRF cavity developed at Jefferson Lab and evaluated in a dedicated horizontal test cryostat at General Atomics. Peak surface magnetic fields up to 18.4\,mT, corresponding to accelerating gradients of approximately 4.3\,MV/m, were achieved in one of the cells. The results provide key insights into cavity preparation, thin-film coating, mechanical robustness, and cryogenic integration, offering guidance for the continued maturation of compact, conduction-cooled SRF accelerators for industrial irradiation applications.

title: International atomic clock comparison achieving $5\times 10^{-18}$ uncertainty
summary: Two single-ion optical clocks, located in the United Kingdom and in Germany, are compared remotely via a 2220\,km long optical fiber link. Both clocks are based on the ${}^2S_{1/2} (F=0)\leftrightarrow {}^2F_{7/2} (F=3)$ electric octupole (E3) transition in $^{171}\text{Yb}^+$. Using more than $10^6$ seconds of measurement data, we determine a fractional frequency difference of $1.0(4.8)\times 10^{-18}$, demonstrating agreement of the independently developed systems. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first international clock comparison reaching a fractional uncertainty below $5\times 10^{-18}$, an important milestone towards an anticipated optical redefinition of the SI second. The measurement uncertainty is dominated by that of the relativistic redshift correction between the two sites, which includes time-varying gravity potential differences. We exploit the large baseline between the two clocks to search for violations of Lorentz invariance. In the absence of statistically significant modulations, we improve constraints on the Robertson-Mansouri-Sexl parameter $α$ by approximately a factor of five in the uncertainty, and provide limits on corresponding parameters within the Standard-Model Extension framework.

AI.tldr: Two independently developed 171Yb+ single-ion optical clocks in the UK and Germany were compared over a 2220 km fiber link using more than 10^6 s of data, yielding a fractional frequency difference of 1.0(4.8)×10^-18 and improving Lorentz-invariance constraints.
AI.motivation: The work aims to demonstrate remote agreement of independently developed optical clocks at an uncertainty below 5×10^-18, a milestone toward an anticipated optical redefinition of the SI second, and to exploit the long baseline to search for violations of Lorentz invariance.
AI.method: The clocks use the 2S1/2(F=0)↔2F7/2(F=3) electric octupole transition in 171Yb+ and are located in the United Kingdom and Germany. They were compared via a 2220 km optical fiber link using more than 10^6 s of measurement data; the fractional frequency difference was determined, relativistic redshift correction between sites was considered, and Lorentz-invariance violations were searched for through possible modulation signatures.
AI.result: A fractional frequency difference of 1.0(4.8)×10^-18 was found, showing agreement between the independently developed systems. title: Accurate Wichmann-Kroll vacuum polarization calculations with Gaussian basis set
summary: We apply a large Gaussian basis set of size up to $N = 500$ to calculate the all-order Wichmann-Kroll vacuum polarization correction in highly-charged ion. For a hydrogen-like system, this allows us to obtain an accurate correction value with a level of precision comparable to that of traditional methods. We demonstrate that values of effects that can be calculated as the difference between two quantities, such as the nuclear model correction, converge faster than the absolute value of the correction. We discuss the basis extrapolation methods and show their use in estimating the error due to incomplete convergence. Finally, we show an application of the Gaussian basis set to calculation of the vacuum polarization screening correction in lithium-like ions.

AI.tldr: A large Gaussian basis set, up to N = 500, is used to compute the all-order Wichmann-Kroll vacuum polarization correction in highly charged ions; hydrogen-like results reach precision comparable to traditional methods, difference-type quantities converge faster, extrapolation estimates incomplete-convergence error, and the basis is applied to vacuum polarization screening in lithium-like ions.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to calculate the all-order Wichmann-Kroll vacuum polarization correction in highly charged ions using a large Gaussian basis set and to assess its accuracy, convergence behavior, error estimation, and applicability to related corrections.
AI.method: The authors apply a Gaussian basis set of size up to N = 500 to compute the all-order Wichmann-Kroll vacuum polarization correction. They benchmark the approach for a hydrogen-like system, analyze quantities expressible as differences between two values such as the nuclear model correction, discuss basis extrapolation methods for estimating incomplete-convergence error, and apply the basis to the vacuum polarization screening correction in lithium-like ions.

title: A compact ultracold strontium experiment
summary: We describe a compact and simplified experimental setup for the production of ultracold strontium atoms. Thanks to its low-power oven and coil-free Zeeman slower design, the vacuum system has an overall length of only 40cm including oven, Zeeman slower and all-glass science cell. The oven has a power consumption of 14W at 460°C and produces a collimated flux of 3 10^10at/(s cm^2) at this temperature. The laser system employs master-slave laser architecture throughout and requires neither second-harmonic generation nor tapered amplifiers, reducing cost and complexity. The system has been in continuous use for more than a year.

AI.tldr: A compact, simplified ultracold-strontium apparatus uses a low-power oven, a coil-free Zeeman slower, and an all-glass science cell in a 40 cm vacuum system; master-slave lasers avoid second-harmonic generation and tapered amplifiers, and the setup has operated continuously for over a year.
AI.motivation: To reduce the cost and complexity of producing ultracold strontium atoms through a compact and simplified experimental design.
AI.method: The apparatus combines a low-power oven, a coil-free Zeeman slower, and an all-glass science cell in a vacuum system only 40 cm long. The laser system uses master-slave architecture throughout and requires neither second-harmonic generation nor tapered amplifiers.
AI.result: The described system is compact and simplified, and it has been in continuous use for more than one year. The abstract does not provide further quantitative performance metrics for the ultracold atoms.
AI.conclusion: The reported design lowers cost and complexity while providing a continuously operating source of ultracold strontium atoms.

title: Experimental Optimization of a Cryogenic Buffer Gas Source for Molecular Magneto-optical Traps
summary: Molecular magneto-optical traps (MOTs) are loaded from cryogenic buffer gas beam (CBGB) sources, which produce a large flux of cold molecules. However, only a small fraction of this flux is slowed and captured. Here, we investigate and optimize one of these CBGB sources through a combination of experiment and simulation to maximize the number of molecules loaded into a MOT of CaF molecules. We experimentally determine the range of molecule velocities from the source that are successfully slowed and captured in the MOT, and perform a systematic study of buffer gas source geometries to identify designs that maximize MOT loading. Our observations agree well with Monte Carlo simulations, which provide physical insight into the dynamics within the source and explain how source geometry influences the subset of molecules that are ultimately trapped. These results provide practical design guidelines for optimizing cryogenic buffer gas beam sources used in laser cooling experiments.

AI.tldr: The authors combined experiments and Monte Carlo simulations to optimize a cryogenic buffer gas beam source for loading CaF molecules into a molecular magneto-optical trap, identifying source geometries and velocity classes that improve trapping and deriving practical design guidelines.
AI.motivation: Molecular magneto-optical traps are loaded from cryogenic buffer gas beam sources that produce a large flux of cold molecules, but only a small fraction of this flux is slowed and captured. The work aims to optimize the source to maximize the number of CaF molecules loaded into a MOT.
AI.method: The study combines experiment and simulation. The authors experimentally determine the range of molecule velocities from the source that are successfully slowed and captured in the MOT, systematically study buffer gas source geometries to identify designs that maximize MOT loading, and compare observations with Monte Carlo simulations that model dynamics within the source.

title: UNWRAP: Single-shot phase analysis of bright squeezed vacuum by Newton-ring interferometry
summary: The mean field of pulsed bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) vanishes, but the variance can be large, and is strongly phase-dependent. We employ ultrafast Newton-ring wavefront retrieval and analysis of phase (UNWRAP) to extract the field amplitude and phase profile of each BSV pulse, by Fourier analysis of the interference rings between the BSV and a coherent reference with different phase-front curvature. The concentric ring interference fringes are robust against pointing mismatch and drift, thereby simplifying the analysis. The measured distribution has two phase peaks separated by π radians. The rings sweep the delay between the two pulses, so a single frame can capture the temporal field profile of the BSV, even when it is composed of several temporal modes.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates UNWRAP, an ultrafast Newton-ring wavefront retrieval method, to measure the amplitude and phase profiles of individual pulsed bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) pulses by Fourier analysis of interference rings with a curved coherent reference; it finds two phase peaks separated by π and shows that a single frame can capture the temporal field profile, including multiple temporal modes.
AI.motivation: Pulsed BSV has a vanishing mean field but large, strongly phase-dependent variance, creating a need to extract the field amplitude and phase profile of each BSV pulse despite the absence of a mean field.
AI.method: The authors use ultrafast Newton-ring wavefront retrieval and analysis of phase (UNWRAP), performing Fourier analysis of interference rings formed between the BSV and a coherent reference with different phase-front curvature. The concentric ring fringes are robust against pointing mismatch and drift, and sweeping the delay between pulses allows a single frame to capture the temporal field profile.
AI.result: The measured distribution has two phase peaks separated by π radians. The approach extracts the field amplitude and phase profile of each BSV pulse, and a single frame can capture the temporal field profile even when the BSV is composed of several temporal modes.
AI.conclusion: UNWRAP enables retrieval of the amplitude, phase, and temporal field profile of individual pulsed BSV fields using robust concentric-ring interference, including multimode temporal structure; broader implications are not provided in the abstract.

title: DiffVortex: A quantum-inspired fast solver for incompressible flows
summary: Matrix-product-state (MPS) and quantized tensor-train (QTT) representations offer a promising framework for computational fluid dynamics, with logarithmic run time and memory scaling in mesh size when bond dimensions remain bounded. Existing MPS-based solvers are Eulerian: they compress velocity fields and enforce immersed-body boundary conditions through static masks or body-fitted coordinates. Moving or flexible bodies complicate this approach: deformation requires updating MPS masks every time step, while filamentary vorticity in high-Reynolds-number flows may resist low-rank compression. We propose a complementary approach: compress the Biot--Savart kernel rather than the flow state, evolve vorticity using Lagrangian vortex particles, and represent immersed bodies by bound vortex sheets on Lagrangian surface points. Our main theoretical result is a lifting theorem: QTT rank $r$ of the kernel implies matrix-product-operator (MPO) rank at most $2^d r$ for the corresponding convolution operator in $d$ dimensions, independent of grid resolution. This bound is sharp for our interleaved ordering. With quantics tensor cross interpolation, the moment-to-local stage of a single-level fast multipole method becomes a precomputed tensor-network contraction with quasi-linear complexity, retaining Lagrangian flexibility for immersed bodies. Our PyTorch implementation (\texttt{DiffVortex}) is end-to-end differentiable, runs on GPUs, and handles $6.7\times10^{7}$ particles on a single device. We validate against reference vortex-method results for an impulsively started cylinder and exact and reference solutions for inviscid elliptical vortices. We also demonstrate two-dimensional flows past rigidly moving, multiple, and deforming bodies, including gradients propagated through the full time integration.

title: Hierarchical Response Theory of Electronegativity from Atomic Mean Inner Potential
summary: Electronegativity, introduced by Pauling nearly a century ago, remains chemistry's most widely used yet conceptually ambiguous quantity: is it a fixed atomic constant, or does it depend on chemical environment? We resolve this debate by recasting electronegativity as a continuous response function rooted in the Atomic Mean Inner Potential (AMIP), a quantum-mechanical observable accessible through first-principles calculation and, ultimately, electron holography. Expanding the AMIP with respect to fractional electron removal defines a hierarchy of physically distinct coefficients: the static electronegativity $χ_0$, the Electrostatic Rigidity $\mathcal{R}$---whose sign indicates whether an atom hardens or softens upon oxidation---and the Electrostatic Anharmonic Modulus $\mathcal{A}$. A logarithmic-derivative decomposition links these coefficients to two competing microscopic channels, electronic screening loss and geometric volume collapse, whose balance governs the response of all 102 elements. This competition produces a systematic dichotomy between softening main-group elements and hardening d-block elements, two scaling laws within the transition series (closed-shell stiffening and principal quantum softening), and two anomalies: a pronounced exchange-driven effect at half-filled d$^{5}$ configurations and a near-perfect cancellation in Ce. It also resolves the long-standing Cs--Fr controversy, identifying Fr as a critical element whose near-boundary response is amplified fivefold by relativistic contraction of the 7s orbital. The framework reproduces the classical Allen, Pauling, and Mulliken scales as well as Lewis acidity trends, and makes three falsifiable experimental predictions. It transforms electronegativity from a lookup-table number into a predictive, hierarchically structured quantum descriptor.

AI.tldr: The paper recasts electronegativity as a continuous, environment-dependent response function derived from the Atomic Mean Inner Potential, yielding a hierarchy of quantum descriptors that explains periodic trends and anomalies across all 102 elements and reproduces classical electronegativity scales.
AI.motivation: To resolve the long-standing conceptual ambiguity over whether electronegativity is a fixed atomic constant or depends on chemical environment, and to transform it from a lookup-table quantity into a predictive quantum descriptor.
AI.method: The authors define electronegativity via the Atomic Mean Inner Potential (AMIP), an observable accessible by first-principles calculation and electron holography, and expand it with respect to fractional electron removal to obtain static electronegativity χ0, Electrostatic Rigidity R, and Electrostatic Anharmonic Modulus A. title: Tractable Inference with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
summary: Machine-learning surrogates in computational science often require not only accurate predictions but also expectations, variances, conserved integrals, and normalization constants. Conventional neural networks, including Kolmogorov--Arnold networks (KANs), generally evaluate these quantities through Monte Carlo sampling or multidimensional quadrature, making repeated inference costly, particularly in high dimensions. We introduce KANs with Tractable Operators for Uncertainty and Constraints (TOUCKANs), whose finite-degree polynomial outer functions yield a decomposable sum--product representation. Under factorizing input measures, expectations and higher moments then reduce algebraically to deterministic recursions over one-dimensional leaf integrals. Independent and shared inner-block variants form a parameter-efficiency hierarchy, and a universal-approximation proof for its most restricted member extends to the complete class. The same deterministic operators allow conserved integrals and normalization to be imposed throughout training. Across uniform and Gaussian benchmarks through 50 dimensions, deterministic mean and variance errors remained below the median fixed-budget Monte Carlo errors in every case. TOUCKANs also conserved Cahn--Hilliard mass to machine precision and imposed normalization and orthogonality through deterministic moments, enabling joint computation of the lowest four Schrödinger eigenpairs in two, three, and five dimensions. TOUCKANs therefore connect KAN approximation with tractable probabilistic circuits, making statistical operators and integral constraints directly available within an expressive neural surrogate.

AI.tldr: TOUCKANs are KAN-based neural surrogates with decomposable polynomial structure that compute expectations, moments, conserved integrals, and normalization deterministically, avoiding repeated Monte Carlo or quadrature while retaining expressive approximation.

title: Semiclassical molecular dynamics simulations of electromagnetically induced transparency cooling of 2D and 3D ion crystals in a Penning trap
summary: Motional modes of trapped-ion crystals in Penning traps can now be cooled to near their ground states via electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) cooling. Numerical simulations are valuable tools for interpreting EIT cooling results and optimizing experimental protocols, but existing molecular dynamics codes are limited to the simulation of Doppler cooling. In this work, we fill this gap by implementing a semiclassical model of EIT cooling in a novel MD code. By simultaneously evolving the ions' internal quantum states and classical motion, we are able to calculate the instantaneous EIT laser forces acting on the ions. We first validate our code by comparing the single-ion cooling rate to fully quantum simulation results. Next, we analyze cooling of the drumhead modes in planar ion crystals, quantifying the effects of planar ion motion and a finite laser beam width. Finally, we demonstrate efficient EIT cooling of the axial modes in 3D ellipsoidal crystals containing up to 500 ions. Such crystals are a promising platform for future quantum sensing experiments with enhanced sensitivity. We find that the mode spectra of 3D crystals can be engineered to enable sympathetic cooling of the low-frequency $\boldsymbol{E}\times\boldsymbol{B}$ modes. This numerical framework provides a powerful tool for modeling sub-Doppler cooling techniques and for optimizing future quantum sensing and quantum information experiments.

title: Model-based computational study of reactive fluid systems using transfer operator methods
summary:
In many industrial applications one aims for the design of efficient chemical reactions. This is often done using experimental analysis of the reactors in combination with numerical twins. However, the simultaneous modeling of flow, mixing and chemical reaction remains a complicated task because the computational costs are still significant and oftentimes prohibitive.
  Here, we model and analyze mixing processes of chemical substances by a transfer operator method using the Lagrangian trajectories of passive particles. In practice, we represent the spatial distributions of the chemical species concentrations by density vectors. These are evolved by means of a stochastic transition matrix, which is obtained as a numerical approximation of a transfer operator. In a further step, we model the reaction of the fluids by specific update rules of the density vectors. The method is applicable for closed and open example systems and different chemical processes such as competitive consecutive reactions. We demonstrate that the dynamic processes are reflected well by this method. Furthermore, we evaluate the interdependence of the reaction fronts with Lagrangian coherent structures which we define using set-oriented methods that also work well on three dimensional data.

Spatial distributions of chemical species concentrations are represented as density vectors and evolved with a stochastic transition matrix obtained as a numerical approximation of a transfer operator. Chemical reactions are modeled through specific update rules for the density vectors. The approach is applied to closed and open example systems and to different chemical processes, including competitive consecutive reactions. Reaction fronts are also evaluated in relation to Lagrangian coherent structures defined using set-oriented methods that are stated to work well on three-dimensional data.

title: Geometry-controlled zeros of resonant Kelvin-wave conversion in four spatial dimensions
summary: Kelvin waves carry energy along vortices, but their resonant interactions contain information that is absent from the linear spectrum. We identify a geometry that exposes this information on a vortex surface in four spatial dimensions. Perpendicular incoming waves cancel the complete local-area four-wave coupling, leaving the finite nonlocal interaction mediated by the surrounding fluid. This interaction restores conversion at generic wave-number ratios, yet changes sign and vanishes at a selected ratio while momentum and frequency remain exactly matched. Matching to Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) theory, including the microscopic core response, establishes a zero of the full coupling at every sufficiently small nonzero wave number, with ratio tending to $λ_*\simeq1.469$. Finite-grid GP coefficients exhibit a sign reversal for the same resonant quartets. Separate coherent-mixing calculations and weak-probe spectra connect the coupling sign to the generated-wave phase and the ordering of reflection-even and reflection-odd modes. The resulting suppression removes a leading channel for changing propagation directions without changing the paired wavelengths. These results isolate a nonlinear effect of the surrounding flow that local tension misses, providing a microscopic benchmark for vortex-wave theories and a starting point for studying angular redistribution beyond the Kelvin spectrum.

title: Pushing beyond the memory barrier in propagation algorithms with randomization
summary: Performant classical tools for simulating quantum circuits are important for benchmarking and supporting upcoming quantum devices. Pauli propagation offers promising capabilities, but deep circuits usually cause a rapid growth in the number of Pauli strings and can quickly exhaust the available memory. In this work, we introduce a randomized protocol that combines a specialized resampling schedule, merging, and a controlled amount of bias to keep the propagating Pauli sum within any prescribed memory budget. Additional computational resources can then be spent on embarrassingly parallel repetitions that systematically improve the estimate. Building on the open-source library PauliPropagation.jl, we show that 1) increasing memory of each simulation reduces the error systematically more than outside averaging, 2) resampling just enough to apply the next gate delays variance accumulation and gives better error-per-time trade-offs than more aggressive resampling, and 3) a small, controlled bias is crucial in cutting down variance and pushing far beyond unbiased randomization. The resulting framework can reproduce deterministic calculations while requiring several orders of magnitude less memory.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a randomized Pauli-propagation protocol that uses a specialized resampling schedule, merging, and a controlled amount of bias to constrain the propagating Pauli sum to a prescribed memory budget, with parallel repetitions improving estimates. Experiments built on PauliPropagation.jl show memory scaling, variance, and bias trade-offs, and reproduce deterministic calculations with orders-of-magnitude less memory.

AI.method: The authors propose a randomized protocol combining a specialized resampling schedule, merging of Pauli strings, and a controlled amount of bias to keep the propagating Pauli sum within any prescribed memory budget. Additional computational resources are used for embarrassingly parallel repetitions to systematically improve the estimate. The implementation builds on the open-source library PauliPropagation.jl.

AI.conclusion: A randomized, memory-bounded Pauli-propagation framework with controlled bias, merging, and tailored resampling can improve estimation efficiency and reproduce deterministic calculations at substantially lower memory cost, although the abstract does not provide specific quantitative benchmarks.

title: Acoustic control of Rayleigh-regime liquid-jet breakup using a through-hole MHz transducer
summary: This experimental study demonstrates MHz-order acoustic control of Rayleigh-regime liquid-jet breakup using a compact through-hole lithium niobate thickness-mode transducer integrated at the nozzle exit and driven near its 6.7 MHz resonance. Jet dynamics were measured by high-speed shadowgraphy at 50,000 fps, and breakup lengths were obtained from instantaneous jet-length records using an autocorrelation-based method that identifies statistically separated breakup events. Acoustic actuation produced visible interfacial corrugations and reduced the normalized breakup length, $L_b/d$, for both water and glycerol--water jets. In water, the response was threshold-like at low Weber number and weakened as the jet velocity increased to We ~ 50. A reduced-order threshold correlation, fit to the water amplitude and velocity sweeps, captured this abrupt shortening and the subsequent loss of actuation efficacy. More viscous glycerol--water mixtures shortened immediately at low forcing, indicating a distinct acoustic-coupling regime rather than a universal collapse of the water response. A wetting-control experiment showed that liquid spreading at the nozzle base can also shorten the jet, so the measured response reflects coupled radiation-pressure forcing, capillary-wave feedback, and wetting-mediated disturbance injection. title: Automated Discovery of Physically Interpretable Subgrid Length Scales for Detached Eddy Simulation via Agentic AI
summary: Traditional turbulence-model development relies heavily on expert knowledge and is time-consuming. This study develops an agentic AI framework, DEScover (automated Discovery of DES closures), to explore subgrid length scales for detached eddy simulation (DES). The user provides only a modeling idea: the length scale is the grid width normal to the local vortex axis. Four large language model (LLM) agents then propose, review, implement, and evaluate candidate formulations and generate scripts for CFD simulations. The Discovery Agent infers the vortex axis from various vortex-identification methods. The candidates are tested on four cases spanning canonical and engineering flows: a flat plate, a backward-facing step, a free shear layer, and an iced airfoil. For all test cases, the best candidate consistently outperforms the standard length scale based on the maximum cell size. Its accuracy is similar to, or slightly better than, that of the expert-designed shear-layer-adapted length scale. Each agentic discovery run takes about 25 minutes on average, excluding the CFD simulations. These results show that LLM-based reasoning can significantly accelerate the discovery of physically interpretable turbulence models and reduce reliance on manual expert formulation.

title: Dynamics of liquid jet breakup and droplet size distribution in a crossflow airstream
comment: 38 pages, 19 figures, Accepted in Journal of Fluid Mechanics
summary: The fragmentation of a liquid jet in a crossflowing airstream arises from a complex interplay between aerodynamic forcing and interfacial instabilities acting across a wide range of length scales. We examine the spatial evolution of droplet size distributions along the jet trajectory using a combination of high-speed shadowgraphy and digital in-line holography, allowing simultaneous characterization of jet morphology and volumetric droplet size distributions. The results demonstrate a clear progression of breakup mechanisms, from near-field bag rupture to downstream rim, ligament, and node disintegration, each associated with distinct characteristic length scales. This evolution is reflected in the droplet size distributions, which broaden and become increasingly polydisperse downstream relative to the near-field distributions. By systematically varying the liquid-jet and airstream Weber numbers, we identify distinct breakup modes, and construct a regime map that delineates the column-breakup, isolated-bag-breakup, and interacting-bag regimes. Furthermore, by incorporating the dominant instability mechanisms, including Rayleigh-Taylor and Rayleigh-Plateau instabilities associated with the observed column, bag, and multi-bag breakup modes, we develop a theoretical framework for jet atomization in crossflow. The framework relates instability wavelengths to characteristic droplet sizes, and reasonably captures the experimentally observed trends. We found that stronger aerodynamic forcing induces earlier breakup, decreases the characteristic instability length scales, and generates finer droplets dispersed over a wider spatial region. Overall, the study establishes a quantitative relationship between instability-driven fragmentation dynamics and droplet size distributions, thereby connecting interfacial instabilities with measurable spray characteristics.

title: Phonon-assisted free-electron recoil control and mechanical sensing
summary: Mechanical vibrations are fundamental to a wide range of physical phenomena and technologies, yet their ability to actively shape free-electron dynamics remains largely unexplored. Here we theoretically show how an optomechanical membrane provides a phonon-assisted optical interface for controlling free-electron recoil and sensing localized forces. Transverse membrane motion scatters cavity light into high-momentum evanescent sidebands that enable phase-matched interaction with electrons traveling in vacuum. Beyond supplying momentum for phase matching, the vibration amplitude controls the electron-light interaction strength and redistributes electron populations among recoil orders. External forces that perturb the vibration are thereby encoded in the electron recoil spectrum. Under the modeled conditions, electron readout of localized stochastic forces can yield a higher signal-to-noise ratio than a Gaussian optical homodyne benchmark at equal detected probe rates. These results provide a theoretical basis for mechanically reconfigurable free-electron optics and mode-selective mechanical sensing.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically proposes using an optomechanical membrane to create a phonon-assisted optical interface that controls free-electron recoil and senses localized forces, with modeled electron readout outperforming a Gaussian homodyne benchmark.
AI.motivation: Mechanical vibrations are ubiquitous, but their capacity to actively shape free-electron dynamics is largely unexplored. The work aims to establish a mechanism for controlling free-electron recoil and sensing localized forces via mechanical motion.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze an optomechanical membrane whose transverse motion scatters cavity light into high-momentum evanescent sidebands. title: Computational and experimental study of multi-grain-size sediment transport and sorting process
summary: Successful prediction of the interaction between turbulent flows and river ecosystems is essential for flood management, development of mitigation strategies, and infrastructure protection. Natural riverbeds consist of bed materials of multiple grain sizes that interact with turbulence differently, leading to spatial classification of particle sizes. Such particle sorting processes can only be captured by models capable of handling multiple grain sizes. We present a numerical framework that couples large-eddy simulation with a multi-grain-size sediment transport module to track multiple grain size classes, their local fractions within the bed-load layer, and bed evolution. A laboratory experiment was conducted in a flume with multi-size bed material to examine sediment particle redistribution and sorting. Measured sediment grain size distributions and bed elevations were used to validate the numerical framework. The results of the multi-grain-size sediment transport model for bed deformation were then compared against those of a uniform sediment transport model, demonstrating that the former reduces the prediction errors relative to the experimental measurements from 37.98 to 3.83 percent for maximum scour depth and from 48.35 to 11.54 percent for maximum deposition height. The validated numerical framework was also applied to large-scale meandering rivers with multi-grain bed material, simulating their bed deformation and sediment sorting. The simulation results revealed the formation of particle sorting patterns in meandering rivers, with coarser and finer sediment particles accumulating near the erosional depression (scour) and depositional (point bar) regions, respectively. These findings support the coupled framework's ability to predict sediment particle sorting and highlight the importance of representing bed material heterogeneity in numerical modeling of meandering rivers.

AI.tldr: A large-eddy simulation framework coupled with multi-grain-size sediment transport was developed and validated against flume experiments, then applied to meandering rivers to predict bed deformation and sediment sorting.
AI.motivation: Predicting turbulent flow–river ecosystem interactions is important for flood management, mitigation strategies, and infrastructure protection, but natural riverbeds contain multiple grain sizes whose sorting cannot be captured by models limited to uniform sediment.
AI.method: The authors coupled large-eddy simulation with a multi-grain-size sediment transport module that tracks multiple grain-size classes, their local fractions in the bed-load layer, and bed evolution. title: Electrically Pumped Quadratic-Soliton Mode-Locked Laser in Lithium Niobate Nanophotonics
summary: Femtosecond mode-locked lasers are the workhorse of modern photonics, enabling optical atomic clocks, frequency combs, precision spectroscopy, and ultrafast signal processing. Bringing them onto nanophotonic chips promises miniaturized ultrafast systems, yet combining femtosecond pulse generation with electrical pumping remains a major challenge, rooted in a trade-off between the speed and energy efficiency of mode-locking mechanisms. Kerr-based mechanisms offer nearly instantaneous response but typically require high intracavity peak powers that are difficult to achieve with nanophotonic-compatible semiconductor gain. Conversely, semiconductor saturable absorbers enable strong nonlinear responses at low energies but are limited by their slow carrier dynamics. Here we break this trade-off by introducing quadratic-soliton mode-locking based on a quadratic nonlinear interferometer (QNLI): an effective saturable absorber built from cascaded second-order nonlinearity in periodically poled lithium niobate nanophotonics, with a measured sub-20 fs response time. Through hybrid integration with an electrically pumped semiconductor gain element, we demonstrate a self-starting quadratic-soliton mode-locked laser with femtojoule pulse energies, operating in single- and multiple-soliton states. Quadratic solitons arise through the QNLI's dissipative and dispersive nonlinear response, which we confirm with a modified complex Ginzburg-Landau equation in agreement with measurements. By combining soliton formation with intracavity electro-optic modulation, we generate 750 fs pulses with flat-top spectra. Our engineerable, ultra-energy-efficient, electrically powered laser provides the critical source for fully integrated ultrafast photonic circuits in lithium niobate nanophotonics that natively offers electro-optic control, quadratic wavelength conversion, pulse compression, and spectral broadening.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces quadratic-soliton mode-locking using a quadratic nonlinear interferometer (QNLI) in periodically poled lithium niobate nanophotonics, hybrid-integrated with an electrically pumped semiconductor gain element, to realize a self-starting femtosecond mode-locked laser with femtojoule pulses and electro-optic generation of 750 fs flat-top pulses.

title: Monocular 3D bubble reconstruction: DNS-informed ray tracing and deep learning
summary:
Bubble size, depth, and spatial distribution govern transport and uniformity in multiphase flows. A single shadowgraphic view cannot separate bubble diameter from focal-plane displacement, as image signatures depend on both, while multicamera systems add optical access, calibration, and cost. We develop a single-camera physics-guided framework combining direct numerical simulation (DNS), validated Monte Carlo ray tracing, preprocessing, and focus-conditioned multitask deep learning to recover three-dimensional bubble position and physical-equivalent diameter from two-dimensional shadowgraphs.
  DNS-resolved bubble label images rendered at multiple focal-plane settings. The ray tracer reproduces shadowgraphic signatures with errors below $3\%$ (intensity), $1\%$ (apparent size), $15\%$ (blur), $6\%$ (numerical aperture), and $4\%$ (edge-spread-function shape), running $\sim30\times$ faster than the CPU implementation. The dataset has $900$ frames and $87{,}728$ labeled instances, partitioned by DNS timestamp to prevent leakage and expanded to over $10^{5}$ crops by broad-depth controlled-density rendering. A multitask network predicts signed depth and diameter from crops and focal-plane coordinates, achieving $\sim97.6\%$ normalized depth accuracy on held-out data; a closed-loop DNS-to-image-to-reconstruction test of $180$ bubbles gives diameter error below $9.71\%$ ($\sim90.29\%$ accuracy). On experimental images at four radial planes ($142$--$971$ bubbles each), PDF overlap is $68\%$--$92\%$ and log-PDF correlation is $0.72$--$0.87$. At the focal reference plane ($11{,}679$ bubbles), overlap is $\sim86\%$, correlation is $0.93$, and full-distribution, $D_{99.8}$, and composite errors are below $7.7\%$, increasing with focal-plane distance and defining a recoverability limit. Without stereoscopic hardware, the framework offers a scalable diagnostic for dense bubbly flows.

The network reaches about 97.6% normalized depth accuracy on held-out data. In a closed-loop test of 180 bubbles, diameter error is below 9.71% (about 90.29% accuracy). title: Broadband Mid-Wave Infrared Imaging Enabled by All-Silicon Hyperboloid Metalens
summary: The mid-wave infrared (MWIR, 3-5 microns) is indispensable for thermal sensing, gas detection, long-range imaging, and free-space optical communications. Meta-optics offer a compact, lightweight, and potentially low-cost alternative to conventional refractive optics, making them attractive for size, weight, and power (SWaP)-constrained systems. However, their strong chromatic dispersion has largely restricted imaging to narrow spectral bands. Here, we demonstrate broadband imaging across the full 3-5 micron MWIR band using a single-layer silicon metasurface coupled with computational reconstruction. Remarkably, the reconstruction model is adapted using only four image captures, overcoming large training data requirements and enabling broadband image recovery despite the strongly wavelength-dependent optical response. In contrast to approaches that engineer complex, dispersion-optimized metalens profiles for broadband operation, our method leverages the wavelength-dependent information encoded by a simple 2cm diameter hyperboloid metalens. We show that this metasurface captures sufficient broadband intensity information for computational reconstruction across the entire MWIR band. These results establish a simple route toward broadband computational meta-optics without requiring broadband achromatic metalens designs, offering a promising platform for compact MWIR imaging systems.

AI.tldr: A single-layer 2 cm silicon hyperboloid metalens combined with computational reconstruction enables broadband imaging across the full 3–5 µm mid-wave infrared band; the reconstruction model is adapted using only four image captures, avoiding complex achromatic metalens designs.
AI.motivation: The mid-wave infrared is important for thermal sensing, gas detection, long-range imaging, and free-space optical communications. Meta-optics can reduce size, weight, and power relative to conventional refractive optics, but strong chromatic dispersion has generally limited metalens imaging to narrow spectral bands. The paper aims to enable broadband mid-wave infrared imaging without requiring complex, dispersion-optimized broadband achromatic metalens profiles.
AI.method: The authors use a simple single-layer silicon metasurface—a 2 cm diameter hyperboloid metalens—and leverage the wavelength-dependent information it encodes, rather than engineering a complex dispersion-optimized metalens. Broadband image recovery is performed computationally, and the reconstruction model is adapted using only four image captures, reducing training-data requirements. title: Online Seakeeping Forecast Coupling System Identification With Nonlinear Pseudo Spectral Potential-Flow

title: Passive Phase-Aware Hadamard Decoding: Analytical and Machine-Learning Approaches

title: Swarmlet: a GPU-resident reformulated vortex particle method for coupled multirotor aerodynamics and flight dynamics
summary: We present Swarmlet, a GPU solver for the unsteady aerodynamics and flight dynamics of one or many multirotor vehicles. title: Observation of Size-dependent Optical Modes and Confinement in Fin Cavities using Angle-Resolved Cathodoluminescence

summary: We observe novel optical fringes and emission coherence in laterally formed semiconductor fins using wavelength- and angle-resolved cathodoluminescence (WARCL). Finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations confirm that the observed fringes originate from internal reflections among the fin facets, consistent with a Fabry-Pérot (FP) cavity model where the cavity length determines the fringe spacing. FDTD also reveals a transition from multi-mode to single-longitudinal-mode behavior in 200-nm fins, consistent with experimentally observed fringe narrowing. Increasing fin length from 10 μm to 30 μm compresses fringe spacing via longer round-trip paths. Conversely, tilting the fin end-facet from 90° to 45° reduces the effective light path length, increasing the incoherent optical emission. Remarkably, this loss can be offset by adjusting the fin length-to-height ratio. Results suggest WARCL is a robust in-situ method for direct characterization of individual dielectric nanocavities, mapping their modal profiles and light directionality as a function of geometry for custom design of nanoscale optical sources and waveguides.

title: Hydrodynamics of microalgae in sea spray
summary: Airborne transmission of biological matter is likely to cause numerous respiratory distress in coastal populations during certain harmful algal blooms. While we know that dissolved algal toxins aerosolize, the contribution of particle-associated toxins is still unknown. Exchange of particulate matter between ocean and atmosphere is driven by sea spray: microplastics and bacteria aerosolize in jet droplets, following the bursting of air bubbles. However, current models for particle capture only consider surface effects, which fail to explain how large microalgal cells (5-50 um) can be entrapped in jet drops (100-800 um). Here, we demonstrate with a variety of species that microalgae are consistently captured in jet drops, and derive a new particle capture model based on the hydrodynamics of the jet. Using the enrichment factor, which measures the increase in concentration in the first jet drop relative to the bulk, we uncover two regimes. The transition between regimes strongly depends on cell size. In addition, we highlight the dynamics of particles within the jet and derive an enrichment model based on hydrodynamics rather than surface considerations. This work widens and generalizes established results on bacterial and microplastic entrapment in jet drops, resolving discrepancies found in the literature. Finally, we demonstrate that sea spray can aerosolize toxic Ostreopsis cf. ovata cells. This reveals a potential particulate pathway for airborne toxicity during harmful algal blooms and raises the question of the relative contribution of particles to that of dissolved toxins.

title: Fast2Peak: High-Fidelity Restoration Algorithm by Single-Pixel Masking towards Real-Time Spectral Measurements

summary: Improving the temporal and spatial resolution of spectroscopy inevitably reduces the photons available to each measurement, pushing rapid measurements into photon-starved conditions where weak spectral features are obscured by stochastic background noise. Here, we present Fast2Peak (F2P), a self-supervised Transformer framework that transforms the spectral restoration task into a context-prediction problem. Given that physically constrained spectral signals exhibit strong local continuity, whereas the stochastic noise fluctuates randomly and does not possess the continuity across neighboring spectral pixels, single-pixel masking enables F2P to restore the predictable signal structure while suppressing unpredictable fluctuations even without clean reference spectra. Unlike conventional offline spectral restoration, F2P achieves high-fidelity restoration within milliseconds, enabling real-time "acquire-and-process" operation. We demonstrate this capability in time-resolved electrochemical SERS and hyperspectral Raman imaging, where spectral restoration is performed during data acquisition. In addition, F2P has demonstrated its robust generalization across different instruments and spectral modalities, including Raman, NMR, XRD and FTIR.

title: Synchronization-Induced Limit Cycles and Hysteresis in Spinor Exciton-Polaritons
summary: We study the nonlinear dynamics of spinor exciton-polaritons in resonantly pumped microcavities. title: Extending AMIRAL's blind deconvolution of Adaptive Optics corrected images with Markov chain Monte Carlo methods
summary: Adaptive optics (AO) corrected image restoration is particularly difficult, as it suffers from the lack of knowledge on the point spread function (PSF) in addition to usual difficulties. In this communication, we propose a new restoration method, which consists in choosing the Minimum Mean Square Error (MMSE) estimator and computing the latter thanks to a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm. We validate our method by means of realistic simulations, in two very different contexts: an astronomical observation on VLT/SPHERE and a ground-based LEO satellite observation on a 1.52m telescope. Finally, we present results on experimental images for both applications.

title: Quasi-Phase-Matched Second Harmonic Generation in Poling-Free Lithium Niobate Microrings with Surface Molecular Pattern

title: Light pulse propagation through a dielectric slab. I. Retarded integral equations and their local finite-difference solution
summary: We describe the propagation of a nonresonant light pulse normally incident on a thin dielectric slab using an integral-equation approach to electromagnetism. For a slab thick enough that the front- and back-surface reflections are temporally separated, the front-surface reflectivity extracted from the simulation agrees with the Fresnel formula to within 1 percent, and the back-surface echo appears at exactly the expected round-trip delay. For a slab thinner than one optical cycle, the multiply-reflected wavelets overlap and interfere, and a full space-time map of the field directly visualizes the build-up of thin-film-like interference in the time domain. The material parameters used here are illustrative rather than fitted to measured data, and the numerical scheme is verified by an explicit grid-convergence study. In a companion paper (Paper II) the retarded integral equations are solved directly, without the local reformulation, and the two independent numerical solutions are shown to agree.

title: Higher-Order Flatband-Touching Points Mediate Unconventional Bulk-Boundary Correspondence
summary: The bulk-boundary correspondence establishes a fundamental connection between bulk band topology and the emergence of boundary states, underpinning topological phenomena across electronic, acoustic, photonic, and many other wave systems. A broad class of singular flatband systems, however, exhibits an unconventional form of bulk-boundary correspondence, in which robust boundary modes (RBMs) originate from flatband-touching points (FBTPs) and the real-space topology associated with incomplete sets of compact localized states (CLSs), rather than conventional momentum-space bulk topological invariants. Here, we experimentally demonstrate unconventional bulk-boundary correspondence in a photonic cross-bedded Kagome-like lattice featuring a higher-order FBTP formed by the touching of two degenerate flatbands and a dispersive band. Using continuous-wave laser writing, we observe shape-preserving propagation of both bulk CLSs and boundary RBMs. Remarkably, unlike previously reported flatband systems, the RBMs retain their boundary localization under input-field perturbations involving both singular and nonsingular CLSs, revealing an unconventional boundary response associated with the higher-order FBTP in this lattice. Our results establish the Kagome-like lattice as a new platform for exploring flatband physics and unconventional bulk-boundary correspondence, with potential applications in wave localization, flatband lasers, and other emerging topological photonic devices.

title: Microlens-Integrated Grating Couplers for Efficient Free-Space Coupling in Silicon Photonics
summary: Grating-coupler arrays are used to couple free-space light into photonic chips, but the space required for tapers and routing waveguides limits their optical fill factor. Microlens arrays can increase the effective fill factor by collecting light over a larger area and focusing it onto each grating. Separately fabricated lens arrays, however, require assembly and precise alignment to the chip. Here we integrate refractive microlenses directly with high-efficiency, normal-incidence grating couplers using two-photon polymerization. Each lens has a 100 x 100 um2 aperture and focuses incident light onto the grating. Writing the lens body at coarse resolution and the optical surface at fine resolution reduces the print time from 9 h to 19 min per lens. Under illumination by a Gaussian beam with a 276 um mode-field diameter, a printed lens increases the measured coupled power by a factor of 33 (15.2 dB) relative to the same grating before printing. Loss normalization gives an estimated lens-to-mode efficiency of 68%. The lenses show no measurable change in coupling after three 3 h thermal cycles at 150C. These results support direct printing as an approach to increasing free-space collection while simplifying lens integration in photonic systems.

title: Second-Order Nonlinear Microresonators on Thin-Film Lithium Tantalate
summary: Nonlinear frequency conversion enables coherent light generation in spectral regions that conventional lasers cannot reach directly and is foundational to the generation of squeezed states and correlated photon pairs. Implementing these nonlinear processes in microresonators lowers the required optical power by orders of magnitude but requires two conditions to be met simultaneously across wide optical bandwidths: phase matching between the interacting fields, and an appropriate coupling condition to the resonator both in the fundamental and second harmonic band. While the former can be addressed by quasi-phase matching through periodic poling, coupling two widely separated spectral bands to the resonator is nontrivial because of the wavelength dependence of mode overlap. Here, we demonstrate parametric oscillation and efficient second-harmonic generation in periodically poled racetracks on thin-film lithium tantalate on insulator. The proposed resonators feature bus-ring coupling engineered independently in the two spectral bands via a long synchronous directional coupler. Quasi-phase matching is achieved using sidewall poling that is also wavelength-calibrated and locally adapted to compensate for thickness nonuniformities. Together, these two design elements enable second-order parametric oscillation with an on-chip threshold of 181 uW and 9.8% conversion efficiency, with signal and idler tunable over tens of nanometers by a few hundred megahertz of pump detuning. Our design strategy can be flexibly applied to efficient second-harmonic generation, reaching 25% absolute conversion efficiency at milliwatt pump powers. These results show how the coupling condition is a design variable in second-order nonlinear resonators and establish thin-film lithium tantalate as a competitive platform for efficient and low-power frequency conversion.

title: Unambiguous determination of the THz conductivity in driven YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6+x}$
summary: Mid-infrared pump, THz probe experiments in YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6+x}$ yield evidence of a high-temperature transient state of the material with the optical properties of a superconductor. However, there are ambiguities in the extracted transient c-axis THz optical properties, primarily resulting from the sublinear growth of the THz response with increasing mid-infrared pump fluence. It was proposed that this effect may be related to saturation of the material's response, which would then perturb its spatial profile and lead one to overestimate the induced change in the transient optical properties. Yet, sublinear growth of the signal could also arise from other effects unrelated to saturation, for example from a change in reflectivity or deposition depth for the pump pulses. Here, we remove this ambiguity by experimentally measuring the fluence-dependent complex optical constants at the 15-20 THz frequencies of the pump. We show that the observed sublinear growth is to be attributed in large part to the enhanced reflection and reduced penetration depth of the pump field at high fluences. When taking into account these findings, we confirm the original interpretation of a light-induced superconducting state both qualitatively and quantitatively.

AI.tldr: Mid-infrared pump/THz probe experiments in YBa2Cu3O6+x suggest a transient high-temperature superconducting-like state, but sublinear THz signal growth with pump fluence created ambiguity. Measuring the pump's complex optical constants at 15–20 THz shows that enhanced reflection and reduced pump penetration depth largely explain the sublinear growth, and accounting for this confirms the original light-induced superconducting interpretation.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to resolve ambiguity in the extracted transient c-axis THz optical properties of YBa2Cu3O6+x. Sublinear growth of the THz response with mid-infrared pump fluence could reflect saturation and cause overestimation of the induced optical change, or could arise from unrelated effects such as changed reflectivity or pump deposition depth.

AI.result: The observed sublinear growth is attributed in large part to enhanced reflection and reduced penetration depth of the pump field at high fluences. title: Zero-group-velocity modes in textured steel plates: experiments and elastic modeling
summary: Zero-group-velocity (ZGV) resonances are investigated as a non-contact ultrasonic probe of elastic anisotropy in textured steel plates. Directional laser-ultrasonic measurements were performed on 70% cold-rolled Ti-stabilized interstitial-free steel plates in the full-hard and recrystallized condition. Experimental results were compared with predictions based on effective elastic stiffness tensors derived from X-ray diffraction measurements. Classical Voigt-Reuss-Hill estimates and microstructure-resolved finite-element homogenization reproduce the measured angular dependence of the ZGV frequencies well for both states, with the finite-element KUBC/SUBC bounds considerably narrower than the classical Voigt-Reuss bounds. For the full-hard state, agreement with the texture-based model is obtained only after a recovery treatment. This indicates that dislocations present in the full-hard material contribute to its elastic response, an interpretation that is further supported by theoretical estimations. An identifiability analysis shows that the directional ZGV measurements provide access to at least three independently observable combinations of the stiffness tensor components, and concluding suggestions for application in recrystallization monitoring are provided.

AI.tldr: Directional zero-group-velocity (ZGV) laser-ultrasonic measurements were used to probe elastic anisotropy in 70% cold-rolled Ti-stabilized interstitial-free steel in full-hard and recrystallized states; texture-based elastic models reproduced the measured angular dependence, with full-hard agreement requiring a recovery treatment attributed to dislocation contributions.

title: Optimization of Petal-Shaped Occulters for Exo-Earth Observation
comment: Proceedings of SPIE Astronomical Telescopes + Instrumentation conference, Copenhagen, July 2026
summary: Petal-shaped occulters are giant, formation-flying optical devices designed for use in space astronomy. Their primary function is to block the intense starlight to enable the direct observation of exoplanets, a process challenged by the extreme contrast ratio (lower than 1e-10 for an exo-Earth). This study focuses on optimizing the shape of the occulter in order to significantly reduce Fresnel diffraction. For a circular occulter, the diffraction pattern shows the bright Arago spot. Nevertheless, we construct an apodized occulter as the weighted sum of circular occulters of various diameters, owing to the fact that their diffraction are complex amplitudes which can, with adequate weighting, interfere with each other in such a way as to form a resulting diffraction pattern with a very dark central area. This basis of circular occulters allows the use of a simple analytical form for their Fresnel diffraction. First, occulter diameters are fixed on a regularly sampled linear scale, and the weights are obtained by minimizing a quadratic criterion. An improvement is then obtained using a combined optimization over the weights and the diameters sizes. Eventually, the apodized profile is used to design the petal-shaped occulter for physical imple- mentation constraints. The resulting rejection rates are comparable to the results obtained using SISTER ( http://sister.caltech.edu ), which uses a completely different non-parametric approach.

AI.tldr: This paper optimizes the shape of a petal-shaped space occulter to suppress Fresnel diffraction and block starlight for direct exoplanet observation. It models an apodized occulter as a weighted sum of circular occulters, optimizes the weights and then the diameters, and converts the resulting profile into a petal-shaped design. The achieved rejection rates are comparable to those of SISTER.

title: Characterizing universal topological phases beyond spatial embedding
summary: Although Hamiltonians govern wave-matter interactions, conventional characterizations of topological phases of matter require more than the Hamiltonian alone, relying on global invariants defined on closed reciprocal-space manifolds or local commutation relations with position operators. This spatial dependence precludes a unique characterization of topological phases on an abstract platform, whose Hamiltonian can be defined independently of its spatial embedding. Here we establish a framework for characterizing universal topological phases, grounded in the invariance of topological features under arbitrary Hamiltonian-preserving deformations. We construct a Hamiltonian-based spatial embedding that groups a system's constituents according to their connectivity. This embedding, which reproduces the results of conventional topological diagnostics in established systems, enables a coherent extension of topological phases to complex networks using the Hamiltonian alone, further highlighting exceptional robustness in small-world networks. Our results reshape the conceptual foundations of topological physics by decoupling topological characterization from prescribed physical platforms.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Hamiltonian-only framework for universal topological phase characterization based on invariance under Hamiltonian-preserving deformations, using a connectivity-based spatial embedding that reproduces conventional diagnostics and extends topological phases to complex networks.
AI.motivation: Conventional topological phase characterizations depend on spatial information, such as global invariants on closed reciprocal-space manifolds or local commutation relations with position operators. This spatial dependence prevents a unique characterization of topological phases on abstract platforms whose Hamiltonians can be defined independently of spatial embedding.
AI.method: The authors establish a framework grounded in the invariance of topological features under arbitrary Hamiltonian-preserving deformations. They construct a Hamiltonian-based spatial embedding that groups a system's constituents according to their connectivity, enabling topological characterization using the Hamiltonian alone.

title: Optimized Bragg Grating Liquid Crystal Solar Sail
summary: We have designed a thin 3-layer sun-facing diffractive Bragg reflector comprised of a chiral polymeric liquid crystal film. Using Rigorous Coupled-Wave Analysis (RCWA), the stack was optimized to maximize the transverse radiation pressure force across the wavelength band 0.47 - 1.67 micrometers. The optimized structure operates on a single polarization state of light. A two structure stack, each operating on a different state of polarization, is predicted to provide a transverse momentum transfer efficiency of 51%. This study demonstrates how a wavelength selective Bragg grating may be used both as a sunshade to scatter sunlight away from the Earth, and as a solar sail for maintaining a prescribed orbit (such as the Earth-Sun L1 point) owing to the momentum transfer efficiency.

title: Conditional Imaging for Privacy-Preserving Visual Sensing
summary: Conventional visual sensing faces a fundamental dilemma: information that should remain private today may need to be recovered tomorrow. This challenge is becoming increasingly important as cameras become pervasive in our daily surroundings. Existing safeguards either protect visual content only after an image is formed or suppress information during capture in ways that prevent its later recovery. Here, we show through an information-theoretic analysis that privacy and recoverability cannot be achieved simultaneously in static optical systems. Information preserved in a measurement for later reconstruction also remains available to an observer of that measurement, limiting the privacy such systems can provide. To overcome this limitation, we introduce conditional imaging, an imaging approach that changes the optical state for every captured frame. The measurement alone conceals the scene, while knowledge of the corresponding physical system state enables its reconstruction. We analyze how the optical parameters determine the information that can be recovered and use this analysis to guide the design of a camera prototype. We evaluate the system on a captured dataset of human faces using increasingly powerful attempts to recover the scene, from direct visualization and computational inversion to learned reconstruction and identity recognition. Our experiments show that conditional imaging preserves identity in authorized reconstructions while withholding visual information from observers without access to the system state. By making the physical state of the camera part of the information needed for reconstruction, conditional imaging enables visual information to be protected at the point of capture while remaining recoverable for future authorized use.

Conditional imaging addresses this by changing the camera’s optical state for each frame, so the measurement conceals the scene unless the corresponding physical state is known, enabling authorized reconstruction.

It introduces conditional imaging, which changes the optical state for every captured frame, analyzes how optical parameters determine recoverable information, uses this analysis to guide a camera prototype, and evaluates it on a captured dataset of human faces using direct visualization, computational inversion, learned reconstruction, and identity recognition.
